title: Dinner's on me: entertaining and eating out
subtitle: split the bill, impeccable service, take pot luck
summary: Handle a restaurant meal or a dinner at home in natural English - offering to pay, judging the service, stating your food preferences and playing the host.

lesson.heading: Paying the bill
lesson.text: If you **split the bill**, each person pays for themselves or the bill is divided equally. To say you are paying, use the informal **it's on me** or **let me get this**; the formal version is **we'd like you to be our guest**. And to **wine and dine** someone is to invite them out to good restaurants.

examples.text: **Let me get this**. You can pay next time.
I was **wined and dined** every night by the New York office.

left.label: Informal
examples: Fancy coming with us for lunch tomorrow?
Put your credit card away - dinner's **on me**.

right.label: More formal
examples: Would you like to **join us** for dinner at the City Plaza hotel?
We'd like you to **be our guest**.
Do you have any particular **dietary requirements**?

lesson.heading: Describing service in a restaurant
rows: too confident, too inclined to tell people what to do
makes you feel you do not want to go there again

lesson.heading: Two restaurants compared
lesson.text: A customer compares a new Italian restaurant with an old one: 'In the Bella Roma, the service was **impeccable** and quick; at the Casa Italia it's always a bit **sluggish**. In the new place the waiters are **courteous** and friendly without being **overbearing**.'

examples.text: In the other place they tend to be **sullen** and the service is rather **brusque**, which I find very **off-putting**.
But at Bella Roma they'll **go out of their way** to give you what you want.

lesson.heading: Food preferences
lesson.text: Someone with **a sweet tooth** loves sweet things. Someone watching their weight has to **count the calories** or be **calorie-conscious**. A **portion** is the amount of a food served to one person. **Savoury** means salty in flavour, or flavoured with herbs - the opposite of sweet. A **fussy eater** has very particular demands, and someone **teetotal** never drinks alcohol.

examples.text: I have **a sweet tooth** and can never say no to cakes or biscuits.
I have to **count the calories** these days.
I'll just have a small **portion** of dessert, please - I don't want to **overdo it**.
examples.note: overdo it = eat or drink too much

examples.text: I like to end the meal with something **savoury**, like cheese.
Ben's a bit of a **fussy eater**.
No, thanks, I won't have wine. I'm **teetotal**.

lesson.heading: Entertaining at home
rows: eat what your hosts are eating, nothing special
usually means a bottle of wine
a rather formal dinner with guests
an informal group meeting for a meal or drinks
a second helping of a dish (note the plural)
tell me when I have served or poured enough
nuts, crisps and similar things eaten before a meal
a ready-cooked meal bought to take home

lesson.text: Seconds is always plural - Does anyone want seconds? - and the answer to Say when is simply When!

exercises.prompt: When we eat out as a group, we usually ___ the bill.
exercises.explanation: To split the bill is to divide it equally, or for each person to pay for themselves.

exercises.prompt: Put your credit card away. Dinner's ___ me.
exercises.explanation: Dinner's on me is the informal way of saying I am paying for you.

exercises.prompt: Visitors to the company's head office in London are always ___ and dined at the best restaurants.
exercises.explanation: To wine and dine someone is to invite them out to good restaurants.

exercises.prompt: Which is the more formal way of inviting someone to lunch?
options: Would you like to join us for lunch tomorrow?
Fancy coming with us for lunch tomorrow?
exercises.explanation: Join us is the formal version; fancy coming is informal.

exercises.prompt: Which is the formal way of offering to pay for someone at the theatre?
options: I'd like you to be my guest.
exercises.explanation: Be our guest is the formal way of saying we will pay.

exercises.prompt: No wine for me, thanks. I'm ___.
I don't really like sweet things - I haven't got a sweet ___.
exercises.explanation: To have a sweet tooth is to love sweet things.

exercises.prompt: Before I book the restaurant, do you have any particular dietary ___?
exercises.explanation: Dietary requirements are special needs or things someone cannot eat; it is a formal phrase.

exercises.prompt: Just a small ___ for me, please. I don't want to overdo it.
exercises.explanation: A portion is the amount of a particular food that is served to one person.

exercises.prompt: Sasha is such a ___ eater. It's difficult to find things she likes.
exercises.explanation: A fussy eater has very particular demands when eating.

exercises.prompt: She's become very careful about how many calories she's eating. How would you say that?
exercises.explanation: To be calorie-conscious is to be careful how many calories you eat; you can also say she's counting the calories.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase with the word from the unit that contrasts with it.
Match each meaning with the expression used at home.

pairs.left: eat whatever your hosts are eating, nothing special
tell me when I've poured enough
nuts and crisps before the meal

exercises.statement: A dinner party and an informal get-together are exactly the same thing.
exercises.explanation: A dinner party is a rather formal dinner with guests; a get-together is an informal meeting for a meal or drinks.

exercises.prompt: Is each expression about eating out, or about entertaining at home?
Put this restaurant review sentence in order.
exercises.answer: They'll go out of their way to give you what you want
exercises.explanation: To go out of your way is to do everything possible to help.
